newsitem.title: USA: FASB defends move on derivatives accounting rules.
newsitem.headline: FASB defends move on derivatives accounting rules.

text.p: The Financial Accounting Standards Board said Monday it still wants to finish by year- end controversial derivatives accounting rules, despite recent criticism from a group of top corporate executives.

"The Board has attempted to be as responsive as possible to the competing demands of the various constituencies, while still achieving the primary goal of making financial reports more transparent," wrote FASB Chairman Edmund L. Jenkins, in an August 1 letter to the executives it released Monday.

Last week, the corporate group faulted the accounting board for moving quickly on the rules. It said FASB has not "adequately considered" the wide range of concerns that have been expressed, including the potential impact on the capital markets.

But Jenkins, in his letter sent also to lawmakers and Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt, maintained that investors need better disclosure about the derivatives transactions companies enter into.

"Companies currently omit from their financial statements billions of dollars of transactions in derivative instruments each year," he said. "That makes it difficult for investors to properly evaluate those companies' financial position and risks. The requirements in the Board's proposal would remedy that lack of information."

The latest comments follow a decision in July by FASB to move ahead with a final rule on the accounting of derivatives used as a hedge, even against the wishes of key market players and some top lawmakers.

Although certain issues remain to be resolved, the basic approach to the rules is to require that all derivatives be recognized in the financial statement. Gains and losses resulting from changes in fair values would be accountied for depending on the use of the derivative.
"We hope to publish a final standard by year-end," Jenkins said, maintaining that industry players, among others, would have ample time to comment on the rule proposals.
